import java.io.*;

tabs.label: Complexity & the CP environment
tabs.head: Lecture 1: Complexity & the CP environment
tabs.lead: By the end of this lecture you can look at a problem's limits and know how fast your solution must be, and you have two accepted submissions on CSES.

blocks.title: 1. Why constraints come first
blocks.html:
A computer does roughly 10^8 simple operations per second. Most problems give a 1–2 second time limit. So the input size tells you which algorithms can work before you read the story.

n up toYour solution must be aboutTypical idea
10O(n!)Try every permutation
20O(2^n)Try every subset
500O(n^3)Three nested loops
5,000O(n^2)Two nested loops
10^5 – 10^6O(n log n) or O(n)Sorting, binary search, one pass
10^9+O(log n) or O(1)A formula or repeated halving

Worked check. n = 2 × 10^5. A double loop does about (2 × 10^5)^2 = 4 × 10^10 steps: 400 seconds. Too slow. Sorting does about n log n ≈ 3.5 × 10^6 steps: fine.

blocks.title: 2. Big-O in one minute
blocks.html:
Big-O counts how the work grows as n grows, ignoring constant factors.

  • One loop over n items: O(n)
  • A loop inside a loop: O(n^2)
  • Halving the range each step (binary search): O(log n)
  • Sorting: O(n log n)

blocks.title: 4. Overflow: the silent killer
blocks.html:
A 32-bit int holds values up to about 2.1 × 10^9. Beyond that it wraps around to negative numbers without any error.

int a = 100000, b = 100000;
long long bad  = a * b;            // multiplies as int first: overflow
long long good = 1LL * a * b;      // 10,000,000,000: correct
int a = 100000, b = 100000;
long bad  = a * b;                 // overflow before widening
long good = (long) a * b;          // correct

Rule: if values or sums can pass 2 × 10^9, use long long (C++) or long (Java).

blocks.title: 5. Worked example: Weird Algorithm
blocks.html:
CSES 1068. Start from n. If n is even, divide by 2; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Print every value until you reach 1.

Think first. n ≤ 10^6, but 3n + 1 can grow far beyond that. Values pass 2 × 10^9, so use a 64-bit type.

long long n; cin >> n;
while (true) {
    cout << n << ' ';
    if (n == 1) break;
    n = (n % 2 == 0) ? n / 2 : 3 * n + 1;
}
long n = nextLong();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
while (true) {
    sb.append(n).append(' ');
    if (n == 1) break;
    n = (n % 2 == 0) ? n / 2 : 3 * n + 1;
}
out.println(sb);

blocks.title: 6. Worked example: Missing Number
blocks.html:
CSES 1083. You get n − 1 distinct numbers from 1..n. Find the missing one.

Idea. The numbers 1..n sum to n(n + 1)/2. Subtract what you read. Dry run with n = 5 and input 2 3 1 5: expected 15, actual 11, missing 4.

Alternative. XOR all of 1..n and all inputs. Equal numbers cancel (x XOR x = 0), leaving the missing one. No overflow possible.

Time O(n), memory O(1).

blocks.title: 7. Common mistakes
blocks.html:
• Using int for sums or products that can exceed 2 × 10^9
  • C++: using endl instead of '\n' (very slow on big outputs)
  • Java: using Scanner and System.out.println in loops (TLE on large input)
  • Leaving debug prints in your submission
  • Testing only the sample input

tabs.head: Lecture 2: Standard library toolkit, sorting & comparators
tabs.lead: By the end of this lecture you can pick the right container for a task, sort anything with a custom rule, and catch your own bugs with a stress tester.

Hash vs ordered. Hash containers are faster on average but give no order, and special tests on Codeforces can make them slow. Ordered containers are O(log n) and always safe.

blocks.title: 2. Sorting with your own rule
blocks.html:
Sort intervals by end time, and by start time when ends are equal:

vector<pair<int,int>> v;   // {start, end}
sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
    if (a.second != b.second) return a.second < b.second;
    return a.first < b.first;
});
int[][] v = new int[n][2];   // {start, end}
Arrays.sort(v, (a, b) -> a[1] != b[1]
        ? Integer.compare(a[1], b[1])
        : Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

Rules for comparators:

  • Use < (strict), never <=. A comparator that says a < a breaks sorting.
  • Don't write return a - b;. It overflows for large values. Use Integer.compare(a, b) in Java.
  • Java: Arrays.sort on a primitive int[] can be slowed to O(n^2) by crafted tests. Shuffle the array first, or sort an Integer[] or a List.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Distinct Numbers
blocks.html:
CSES 1621. Count distinct values among n numbers (n ≤ 2 × 10^5).

Way 1: sort and count changes. After sorting, equal values sit together. Count positions where a[i] differs from a[i−1], plus one. O(n log n).

Way 2: hash set. Insert everything; print the size. O(n) average.

sort(a.begin(), a.end());
int cnt = 1;
for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) if (a[i] != a[i-1]) cnt++;
cout << cnt << '\n';
List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>();   // a List sorts with merge sort: no slow worst case
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a.add(nextInt());
Collections.sort(a);
int cnt = 1;
for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) if (!a.get(i).equals(a.get(i - 1))) cnt++;
out.println(cnt);

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Concert Tickets
blocks.html:
CSES 1091. n tickets with prices; m customers arrive one by one, each with a maximum price t. Each buys the most expensive ticket that costs at most t, or gets −1.

What we need. “Find the largest price ≤ t” and “remove one ticket”, both fast, with duplicate prices. That is an ordered multiset.

Dry run. Prices {5, 3, 7, 8, 5}; customers 4, 8, 3.

Customer tLargest price ≤ tRemaining tickets
435, 5, 7, 8
885, 5, 7
3none → −15, 5, 7
multiset<int> s(prices.begin(), prices.end());
for (int t : customers) {
    auto it = s.upper_bound(t);         // first price greater than t
    if (it == s.begin()) { cout << -1 << '\n'; continue; }
    --it;                                // step back: largest price <= t
    cout << *it << '\n';
    s.erase(it);                         // removes ONE ticket
}
TreeMap<Integer, Integer> m = new TreeMap<>();   // price -> count
for (int p : prices) m.merge(p, 1, Integer::sum);
for (int t : customers) {
    Integer k = m.floorKey(t);           // largest price <= t
    if (k == null) { out.println(-1); continue; }
    out.println(k);
    if (m.merge(k, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) m.remove(k);
}

Time O((n + m) log n).

blocks.title: 5. Stress testing your code
blocks.html:
When your solution fails a hidden test, compare it against a slow but obviously correct version on thousands of small random inputs.

  1. gen: prints a random small test (for example n between 1 and 8, values 1..10).
  2. brute: the simplest correct solution, however slow.
  3. sol: your fast solution.
  4. A loop that runs gen, feeds the test to both, and stops at the first different output.
Terminal
for i in $(seq 1 1000); do
  ./gen $i > in.txt
  ./brute < in.txt > b.txt
  ./sol   < in.txt > s.txt
  if ! cmp -s b.txt s.txt; then echo "Mismatch on test $i"; cat in.txt; break; fi
done

This is exactly what you build in Project 0 (due Lecture 4).

blocks.title: 6. Common mistakes
blocks.html:
• C++: s.erase(x) on a multiset deletes all copies of x. Erase an iterator instead.
  • C++: std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) on a set is slow (O(n)). Use s.lower_bound(x).
  • Java: comparing two Integer objects with ==. It fails for values above 127. Use .equals().
  • Java: forgetting to remove a key from a TreeMap multiset when its count reaches 0.

tabs.label: Prefix sums & difference arrays
tabs.head: Lecture 3: Prefix sums & difference arrays
tabs.lead: Precompute running totals once, and every range sum becomes one subtraction.

blocks.title: 1. 1D prefix sums
blocks.html:
Define p[0] = 0 and p[i] = a[1] + … + a[i]. Then

sum(l..r) = p[r] - p[l-1]

Dry run. a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5] gives p = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. sum(2..4) = p[4] − p[1] = 9 − 3 = 6, and 1 + 4 + 1 = 6. Correct.

Why p[0] = 0? It makes the formula work for l = 1 without a special case.

blocks.title: 2. Worked example: Static Range Sum Queries
blocks.html:
CSES 1646. n, q ≤ 2 × 10^5. Answering each query with a loop is up to 4 × 10^10 steps, far too slow. With prefix sums it is O(n + q).

int n, q; cin >> n >> q;
vector<long long> p(n + 1, 0);
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { long long x; cin >> x; p[i] = p[i-1] + x; }
while (q--) {
    int a, b; cin >> a >> b;
    cout << p[b] - p[a-1] << '\n';
}
int n = nextInt(), q = nextInt();
long[] p = new long[n + 1];
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) p[i] = p[i - 1] + nextLong();
while (q-- > 0) {
    int a = nextInt(), b = nextInt();
    out.println(p[b] - p[a - 1]);
}

blocks.title: 3. 2D prefix sums
blocks.html:
P[i][j] = sum of the rectangle from (1,1) to (i,j). Build it with

P[i][j] = a[i][j] + P[i-1][j] + P[i][j-1] - P[i-1][j-1]

and answer a rectangle (y1, x1)–(y2, x2) with

P[y2][x2] - P[y1-1][x2] - P[y2][x1-1] + P[y1-1][x1-1]

The last term is added back because the top-left block was subtracted twice.

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Forest Queries
blocks.html:
CSES 1652. An n × n grid (n ≤ 1000) of . and * (trees). Answer up to 2 × 10^5 “how many trees in this rectangle” queries.

vector<vector<int>> P(n + 1, vector<int>(n + 1, 0));
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    string row; cin >> row;
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
        P[i][j] = (row[j-1] == '*') + P[i-1][j] + P[i][j-1] - P[i-1][j-1];
}
while (q--) {
    int y1, x1, y2, x2; cin >> y1 >> x1 >> y2 >> x2;
    cout << P[y2][x2] - P[y1-1][x2] - P[y2][x1-1] + P[y1-1][x1-1] << '\n';
}
int[][] P = new int[n + 1][n + 1];
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    String row = br.readLine().trim();
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
        P[i][j] = (row.charAt(j - 1) == '*' ? 1 : 0) + P[i-1][j] + P[i][j-1] - P[i-1][j-1];
}
while (q-- > 0) {
    int y1 = nextInt(), x1 = nextInt(), y2 = nextInt(), x2 = nextInt();
    out.println(P[y2][x2] - P[y1-1][x2] - P[y2][x1-1] + P[y1-1][x1-1]);
}

blocks.title: 5. Difference arrays: many range updates
blocks.html:
To add v to every position in l..r, many times, then read the final array:

  1. Keep d of size n + 2, all zeros.
  2. For each update: d[l] += v and d[r + 1] −= v.
  3. At the end, prefix-sum d. Position i holds the total added there.

Dry run. n = 6, updates +5 on [2, 4] and +3 on [3, 6]. d[1..7] = [0, 5, 3, 0, −5, 0, −3]. Prefix sums give 0, 5, 8, 8, 3, 3 for positions 1..6.

Each update costs O(1) instead of O(n).

blocks.title: 6. Prefix and suffix aggregates
blocks.html:
For operations you can't subtract (max, min, product with zeros), build arrays from both ends:

  • pre[i] = best of a[1..i]
  • suf[i] = best of a[i..n]

Then “best of everything except position i” is combine(pre[i−1], suf[i+1]). That is the key to Product of Array Except Self and Maximal Intersection.

blocks.title: 7. Common mistakes
blocks.html:
• A prefix array of size n instead of n + 1
  • int sums when n × max value exceeds 2 × 10^9
  • In 2D, forgetting to add back the top-left corner
  • Forgetting d[r + 1] −= v, or making d too small for r + 1

tabs.label: Two pointers & sliding window
tabs.head: Lecture 4: Two pointers & sliding window
tabs.lead: Two indices that only move forward can replace a double loop, turning O(n^2) into O(n).

blocks.title: 1. When does it work?
blocks.html:
Two pointers need a monotone condition. For a window [l, r]: if it is valid, every window inside it is also valid (or, for other problems, every window containing it is). Then you never need to move a pointer backwards.

  • “Longest subarray with sum ≤ t” with positive numbers: monotone. Works.
  • Same question with negative numbers: not monotone. Use prefix sums + hashing (Lecture 5).

blocks.title: 2. Pattern A: opposite ends on a sorted array
blocks.html:
Find two numbers summing to x in a sorted array. Start l at the left, r at the right.

  • sum < x → move l right (need bigger)
  • sum > x → move r left (need smaller)
  • sum = x → found

Each step throws away one candidate for good, so it takes at most n steps.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Sum of Two Values
blocks.html:
CSES 1640. Print the original 1-based positions of two different values summing to x, or IMPOSSIBLE. Sort (value, index) pairs so you don't lose the positions.

vector<pair<long long,int>> v(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { cin >> v[i].first; v[i].second = i + 1; }
sort(v.begin(), v.end());
int l = 0, r = n - 1;
while (l < r) {
    long long s = v[l].first + v[r].first;
    if (s == x) { cout << v[l].second << ' ' << v[r].second << '\n'; return; }
    if (s < x) l++; else r--;
}
cout << "IMPOSSIBLE\n";
long[][] v = new long[n][2];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { v[i][0] = nextLong(); v[i][1] = i + 1; }
Arrays.sort(v, (p, q) -> Long.compare(p[0], q[0]));
int l = 0, r = n - 1;
while (l < r) {
    long s = v[l][0] + v[r][0];
    if (s == x) { out.println(v[l][1] + " " + v[r][1]); return; }
    if (s < x) l++; else r--;
}
out.println("IMPOSSIBLE");

blocks.title: 4. Pattern B: the sliding window template
blocks.html:
l = 0
for r in 0..n-1:
    add a[r] to the window
    while the window is invalid:
        remove a[l] from the window; l = l + 1
    the window [l, r] is valid: update the answer

blocks.title: 5. Worked example: Books
blocks.html:
Codeforces 279B. Book i takes a_i ≥ 1 minutes. You have t minutes and read consecutive books from any start. Maximum number of books = longest window with sum ≤ t.

Dry run. a = [3, 1, 2, 1], t = 5.

long long sum = 0; int l = 0, best = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
    sum += a[r];
    while (sum > t) sum -= a[l++];
    best = max(best, r - l + 1);
}

    sum += a[r];
    while (sum > t) sum -= a[l++];
    best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);

out.println(best);

blocks.title: 6. Worked example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
blocks.html:
LeetCode 3. The window is invalid when some character appears twice.

int lengthOfLongestSubstring(string s) {
    vector<int> cnt(256, 0);
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)s.size(); r++) {
        cnt[(unsigned char)s[r]]++;
        while (cnt[(unsigned char)s[r]] > 1) cnt[(unsigned char)s[l++]]--;
        best = max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    int[] cnt = new int[256];
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
        cnt[s.charAt(r)]++;
        while (cnt[s.charAt(r)] > 1) cnt[s.charAt(l++)]--;
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}

blocks.title: 7. Pattern C: fixed-size windows
blocks.html: For windows of exactly k items: add a[r], and once r ≥ k, remove a[r − k]. Every window is processed in O(1).

blocks.title: 8. Common mistakes
blocks.html:
• Shrinking with if instead of while
  • Recording the answer before the window is valid again
  • Using two pointers when values can be negative
  • Losing original indices when you sort

tabs.label: Hashing & frequency techniques
tabs.head: Lecture 5: Hashing & frequency techniques
tabs.lead: Ask “which earlier value would make the current position an answer?”, then look it up in a hash map in O(1).

blocks.title: 1. Hash maps in one paragraph
blocks.html: A hash map stores key → value pairs in buckets chosen by a hash of the key. Lookups, inserts and updates are O(1) on average. In the worst case (many keys in one bucket) they degrade to O(n). Codeforces sometimes has tests built to cause this. The defences are in section 6.

blocks.title: 2. The key identity
blocks.html:
With prefix sums p, a subarray l..r has sum k exactly when

p[r] - p[l-1] = k ⇔ p[l-1] = p[r] - k

So at each r, the number of good subarrays ending at r equals how many earlier prefixes equal p[r] − k. Keep a map from prefix value to count.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Subarray Sum Equals K
blocks.html:
LeetCode 560, also CSES 1661 Subarray Sums II. Values may be negative, so two pointers don't work.

Dry run. a = [1, 2, 3, −2, 2], k = 3.

The four subarrays: [1,2], [3], [2,3,−2], [3,−2,2].

long long countSubarrays(const vector<long long>& a, long long k) {
    unordered_map<long long, long long> cnt;
    cnt.reserve(1 << 19);
    cnt[0] = 1;                       // the empty prefix
    long long p = 0, ans = 0;
    for (long long x : a) {
        p += x;
        auto it = cnt.find(p - k);    // look up BEFORE inserting p
        if (it != cnt.end()) ans += it->second;
        cnt[p]++;
    }
    return ans;
}
static long countSubarrays(long[] a, long k) {
    HashMap<Long, Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>();
    cnt.put(0L, 1);                   // the empty prefix
    long p = 0, ans = 0;
    for (long x : a) {
        p += x;
        ans += cnt.getOrDefault(p - k, 0);   // look up BEFORE inserting p
        cnt.merge(p, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return ans;
}

blocks.title: 4. Counting equal pairs
blocks.html: If a key appears c times, it forms c(c − 1)/2 pairs. Or count as you go: when the key appears for the c-th time, add c − 1.

blocks.title: 5. Value transforms
blocks.html:
Rewrite the condition so each side depends on one index only.

  • Pairs i < j with a[j] − a[i] = j − i ⇔ a[i] − i = a[j] − j. Count equal values of a[i] − i.
  • Subarrays with sum divisible by n ⇔ two prefixes with the same remainder mod n.

Negative remainders. In C++ and Java, −7 % 3 is −1, not 2. Normalise with ((x % m) + m) % m.

blocks.title: 6. Staying safe from anti-hash tests
blocks.html:
• C++: give unordered_map a randomised hash.
C++
struct SplitMix {
    static uint64_t splitmix64(uint64_t x) {
        x += 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15ULL;
        x = (x ^ (x >> 30)) * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9ULL;
        x = (x ^ (x >> 27)) * 0x94d049bb133111ebULL;
        return x ^ (x >> 31);
    }
    size_t operator()(uint64_t x) const {
        static const uint64_t R = chrono::steady_clock::now().time_since_epoch().count();
        return splitmix64(x + R);
    }
};
unordered_map<long long, int, SplitMix> safeMap;
  • Java: XOR keys with a random salt before inserting, or use a TreeMap (O(log n), always safe).

tabs.lead: A greedy algorithm makes the best-looking choice at each step and never looks back. It is fast and short, but only correct when you can prove it.

blocks.title: 1. How to approach a greedy problem
blocks.html:
1. Propose a rule (“always take the one that ends first”).
  2. Try to break it on tiny inputs (2–4 items). Spend two minutes here.
  3. If it survives, prove it with an exchange argument: take any optimal answer, swap its first choice for the greedy choice, and show it is still valid and no worse.
  4. Only then code it.

CSES 1629. Watch as many whole movies as possible; no two can overlap.

Why earliest end works. Let g end first among all movies. Any optimal schedule starts with some movie f that ends no earlier than g. Replace f by g: g ends even earlier, so it fits before everything else. Same count, still valid.

blocks.title: 3. Sweep line: Restaurant Customers
blocks.html:
CSES 1619. Find the maximum number of customers inside at the same time.

Turn each customer into two events: (arrival, +1) and (leaving, −1). Sort all 2n events by time and keep a running total. The answer is the largest total seen. O(n log n).

vector<pair<int,int>> ev;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int a, b; cin >> a >> b; ev.push_back({a, +1}); ev.push_back({b, -1}); }
sort(ev.begin(), ev.end());
int cur = 0, best = 0;
for (auto& [t, d] : ev) { cur += d; best = max(best, cur); }
int[][] ev = new int[2 * n][];
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ev[2*i] = new int[]{nextInt(), 1}; ev[2*i+1] = new int[]{nextInt(), -1}; }
Arrays.sort(ev, (x, y) -> x[0] != y[0] ? Integer.compare(x[0], y[0]) : Integer.compare(x[1], y[1]));
int cur = 0, best = 0;
for (int[] e : ev) { cur += e[1]; best = Math.max(best, cur); }

The tie rule (−1 before +1) treats someone leaving at time t as gone before someone arriving at t. In CSES 1619 all times are distinct, but other problems depend on this choice.

name: M2 Binary search
title: M2 Binary Search: Student Handbook
intro: Binary search needs only one thing: a yes/no question whose answers go no, no, …, no, yes, yes, …, yes. This module teaches one template for it and uses it everywhere.

tabs.label: Binary search fundamentals
tabs.head: Lecture 7: Binary search fundamentals
tabs.lead: Halving the search range every step finds an answer among 10^9 possibilities in about 30 steps.

blocks.title: 1. The “first true” template
blocks.html:
Suppose ok(x) is false for small x and true from some point on. We want the first x where it is true.

// invariant: ok(lo) is false, ok(hi) is true
while hi - lo > 1:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2
    if ok(mid): hi = mid
    else:       lo = mid
answer = hi

Why it always works:

  • mid is strictly between lo and hi, so the gap shrinks every step and the loop ends.
  • The invariant never breaks, so when the gap is 1, hi is the first true position.
  • If no real value is false, start lo one below the range (a “sentinel”), for example lo = −1 for array indices.

blocks.title: 2. Lower bound and upper bound
blocks.html:
On a sorted array a[0..n−1] with lo = −1 and hi = n:

You wantok(i)a = [1, 3, 3, 5, 8], x = 3
First index with a[i] ≥ x (lower bound)a[i] ≥ x1
First index with a[i] > x (upper bound)a[i] > x3
How many equal xupper − lower2
How many in [L, R]upper(R) − lower(L)
int lb = lower_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), x) - a.begin();
int ub = upper_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), x) - a.begin();
// Java has no lower_bound for arrays: write it once and reuse it
static int lowerBound(long[] a, long x) {
    int lo = -1, hi = a.length;              // a[lo] < x, a[hi] >= x (sentinels)
    while (hi - lo > 1) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        if (a[mid] >= x) hi = mid; else lo = mid;
    }
    return hi;
}

Upper bound is the same with a[mid] > x.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Worms
blocks.html:
Codeforces 474B. Worms are numbered across piles: pile 1 has labels 1..a_1, pile 2 continues from there, and so on. For each label q, print its pile.

Idea. With prefix sums p, pile i holds labels p[i−1] + 1 .. p[i]. The answer is the first i with p[i] ≥ q: a lower bound.

Dry run. a = [2, 7, 3, 4, 9]. p = [0, 2, 9, 12, 16, 25]. Label 1 → pile 1; label 25 → pile 5; label 11 → pile 3.

vector<long long> p(n + 1, 0);
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { long long x; cin >> x; p[i] = p[i-1] + x; }
int m; cin >> m;
while (m--) {
    long long q; cin >> q;
    cout << lower_bound(p.begin() + 1, p.end(), q) - p.begin() << '\n';
}
long[] p = new long[n + 1];
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) p[i] = p[i - 1] + nextLong();
int m = nextInt();
while (m-- > 0) {
    long q = nextLong();
    int lo = 0, hi = n;                       // p[0] = 0 < q, p[n] >= q
    while (hi - lo > 1) { int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1; if (p[mid] >= q) hi = mid; else lo = mid; }
    out.println(hi);
}

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
blocks.html:
LeetCode 33. A sorted array of distinct values was rotated, like [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find the index of target, or −1, in O(log n).

Idea. Cut at mid. At least one half is still sorted. Check whether target lies inside the sorted half's range; if yes go there, otherwise go to the other half.

int search(vector<int>& a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = (int)a.size() - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {                       // left half sorted
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {                                     // right half sorted
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
public int search(int[] a, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (a[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (a[lo] <= a[mid]) {
            if (a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]) hi = mid - 1; else lo = mid + 1;
        } else {
            if (a[mid] < target && target <= a[hi]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

This one uses the classic “closed range” loop because it looks for an exact value, not a first-true position. Use <= in a[lo] <= a[mid] so a two-element range works.

blocks.html:
• Mixing loop styles (lo < hi with hi = mid − 1 from another template)
  • mid = (lo + hi) / 2 overflowing when lo and hi are near 2 × 10^9
  • Java's Arrays.binarySearch on arrays with duplicates: it returns any matching index
  • A linear scan per query when there are 10^5 queries

tabs.label: Binary search on the answer
tabs.head: Lecture 8: Binary search on the answer
tabs.lead: When a problem asks for “the minimum T such that something is possible”, don't compute T directly. Write a check can(T) and binary search over T.

blocks.title: 1. Spot the pattern
blocks.html:
Look for these phrases:

  • “minimum time / speed / capacity needed to…”
  • “minimise the largest…” or “maximise the smallest…”
  • an answer range far too large to try every value (up to 10^9 or 10^18)

Then check that can(T) is monotone: if T works, every bigger T works too.

blocks.title: 2. The recipe
blocks.html:
1. Write can(T), usually a greedy O(n) check.
  2. Pick lo where can(lo) is surely false (or a sentinel such as 0) and hi where can(hi) is surely true.
  3. Run the first-true template from Lecture 7 on T.

Total time: O(n × log(hi − lo)). For a range of 10^18 that's about 60 checks.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Factory Machines
blocks.html:
CSES 1620. Machine i makes one product every k_i seconds; all run in parallel. Minimum time to make t products?

Check. In T seconds machine i makes ⌊T / k_i⌋ products. can(T) = Σ ⌊T / k_i⌋ ≥ t. More time never makes fewer products, so it is monotone.

Bounds. lo = 0 (nothing is made). hi = min(k) × t: the fastest machine alone finishes by then.

Dry run. k = [3, 2, 5], t = 7.

Tmade = T/3 + T/2 + T/5can(T)?
72 + 3 + 1 = 6no
82 + 4 + 1 = 7yes

Answer 8.

Overflow trap. With T near 10^18 and k_i = 1, the sum can pass 64 bits. Stop adding as soon as the total reaches t.

int n; long long t; cin >> n >> t;
vector<long long> k(n);
for (auto& x : k) cin >> x;
auto can = [&](long long T) {
    long long made = 0;
    for (long long x : k) { made += T / x; if (made >= t) return true; }
    return false;
};
long long lo = 0, hi = *min_element(k.begin(), k.end()) * t;
while (hi - lo > 1) {
    long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
    if (can(mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid;
}
cout << hi << '\n';
int n = nextInt(); long t = nextLong();
long[] k = new long[n];
long minK = Long.MAX_VALUE;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { k[i] = nextLong(); minK = Math.min(minK, k[i]); }
long lo = 0, hi = minK * t;
while (hi - lo > 1) {
    long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, made = 0;
    boolean ok = false;
    for (long x : k) { made += mid / x; if (made >= t) { ok = true; break; } }
    if (ok) hi = mid; else lo = mid;
}
out.println(hi);

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Koko Eating Bananas
blocks.html:
LeetCode 875. Piles p_i; each hour Koko eats up to s bananas from one pile. Smallest s to finish within h hours?

can(s) = Σ ⌈p_i / s⌉ ≤ h. Compute the ceiling with integers: (p + s − 1) / s. lo = 0, hi = max(p).

int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
    long long lo = 0, hi = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());
    while (hi - lo > 1) {
        long long s = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + s - 1) / s;
        if (hours <= h) hi = s; else lo = s;
    }
    return (int)hi;
}
public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
    long lo = 0, hi = 0;
    for (int p : piles) hi = Math.max(hi, p);
    while (hi - lo > 1) {
        long s = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, hours = 0;
        for (int p : piles) hours += (p + s - 1) / s;
        if (hours <= h) hi = s; else lo = s;
    }
    return (int) hi;
}

blocks.title: 5. Minimise the maximum: Array Division
blocks.html:
CSES 1085. Split the array into k contiguous parts so the largest part sum is as small as possible.

can(S): walk left to right, start a new part whenever adding the next number would exceed S, and count parts. Feasible if parts ≤ k. lo = max(a) − 1 (a part must hold the biggest element), hi = sum of all.

blocks.title: 6. Ternary search (for reference)
blocks.html: If f(x) goes down and then up (unimodal), compare f(m1) and f(m2) at two inner points and drop the worse third. On integers, a simpler and safer alternative is binary search on the slope: first x with f(x + 1) − f(x) ≥ 0. Avoid both on functions with flat stretches.

blocks.title: 7. Common mistakes
blocks.html:
• int for T, sums or products
  • hi too small (wrong answer) or a sum that overflows (no early stop)
  • A check that isn't monotone, often testing “exactly k” instead of “at most k”
  • Forgetting that a part must be at least max(a) in Array Division

title: M3 Recursion, Backtracking & Bits: Student Handbook
intro: This module teaches you to search through every possibility efficiently, to use integers as sets, and ends with Contest 1.

tabs.label: Recursion, backtracking & meet in the middle
tabs.head: Lecture 9: Recursion, backtracking & meet in the middle
tabs.lead: Backtracking tries every option, but gives up on a branch the moment it can't lead to an answer.

blocks.title: 1. Size the search before you code
blocks.html:
What you generateCountSafe up to about
All subsets of n items2^nn = 20–22
All permutations of n itemsn!n = 9–10
Subsets via meet in the middle2 × 2^(n/2)n = 40

blocks.title: 2. The backtracking template
blocks.html:
solve(state):
    if state is complete: record it; return
    for each choice c that is still valid:
        apply c          # choose
        solve(state)     # recurse
        undo c           # un-choose

The “undo” step is what most bugs forget.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Subsets
blocks.html:
LeetCode 78. For each element, either leave it out or put it in.

vector<vector<int>> res; vector<int> cur;
void go(const vector<int>& a, int i) {
    if (i == (int)a.size()) { res.push_back(cur); return; }
    go(a, i + 1);                                   // leave a[i] out
    cur.push_back(a[i]); go(a, i + 1); cur.pop_back();   // put it in, then undo
}
List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
List<Integer> cur = new ArrayList<>();
void go(int[] a, int i) {
    if (i == a.length) { res.add(new ArrayList<>(cur)); return; }
    go(a, i + 1);
    cur.add(a[i]); go(a, i + 1); cur.remove(cur.size() - 1);
}

The same subsets with a loop: for mask from 0 to 2^n − 1, item i is in the subset when bit i of mask is 1 (Lecture 10).

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Creating Strings
blocks.html:
CSES 1622. Print every distinct rearrangement of a string (length ≤ 8) in alphabetical order.

Sort the string first. In C++, next_permutation steps to the next arrangement in order and skips duplicates for you. In Java, backtrack over letter counts: at each position try each letter that still has copies left.

string s; cin >> s; sort(s.begin(), s.end());
vector<string> out;
do out.push_back(s); while (next_permutation(s.begin(), s.end()));
cout << out.size() << '\n';
for (auto& t : out) cout << t << '\n';
static int[] cnt = new int[26];
static StringBuilder all = new StringBuilder(); static int total = 0;
static void build(char[] cur, int pos) {
    if (pos == cur.length) { all.append(cur).append('\n'); total++; return; }
    for (int c = 0; c < 26; c++) if (cnt[c] > 0) {
        cnt[c]--; cur[pos] = (char) ('a' + c);
        build(cur, pos + 1);
        cnt[c]++;                                   // undo
    }
}
// main: count letters into cnt, call build(new char[n], 0), print total then all

blocks.title: 5. Worked example: Chessboard and Queens
blocks.html:
CSES 1624. Place 8 queens on an 8 × 8 board with some squares reserved, so no two attack each other. Count the ways.

Put one queen per row. Square (r, c) lies on diagonal r + c and anti-diagonal r − c + 7. Three boolean arrays tell you instantly whether a column or diagonal is taken.

string b[8]; bool col[8], d1[15], d2[15]; int ways = 0;
void place(int r) {
    if (r == 8) { ways++; return; }
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
        if (b[r][c] == '*' || col[c] || d1[r + c] || d2[r - c + 7]) continue;
        col[c] = d1[r + c] = d2[r - c + 7] = true;
        place(r + 1);
        col[c] = d1[r + c] = d2[r - c + 7] = false;
    }
}
static char[][] b = new char[8][]; static boolean[] col = new boolean[8], d1 = new boolean[15], d2 = new boolean[15];
static int ways = 0;
static void place(int r) {
    if (r == 8) { ways++; return; }
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
        if (b[r][c] == '*' || col[c] || d1[r + c] || d2[r - c + 7]) continue;
        col[c] = d1[r + c] = d2[r - c + 7] = true;
        place(r + 1);
        col[c] = d1[r + c] = d2[r - c + 7] = false;
    }
}

On an empty board the answer is 92.

blocks.title: 6. Meet in the middle
blocks.html:
Count subsets of n ≤ 40 numbers that sum to x (CSES 1628). 2^40 ≈ 10^12 is too many. Instead:

  1. Split the numbers into two halves of at most 20.
  2. List all 2^20 subset sums of each half.
  3. Sort the second list.
  4. For each sum s in the first list, count how many sums in the second equal x − s (upper bound minus lower bound).

About 2^20 × 20 steps: fast.

blocks.html:
• Forgetting to undo a choice
  • Copying the current list at every step instead of only at complete answers
  • Recursion so deep it overflows the stack
  • Java: storing 2^20 sums as Long objects. Use long[]

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Petr and a Combination Lock
blocks.html:
Codeforces 1097B. Rotate the lock n ≤ 15 times by a_i degrees, each either clockwise or counter-clockwise. Can it end at 0?

Each mask is one choice of directions: bit i = 1 means +a_i, 0 means −a_i. 2^15 = 32,768 masks.

bool ok = false;

blocks.title: 5. XOR tricks
blocks.html:
• x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so equal values cancel.
  • XOR of a range works like a prefix sum: xor(l..r) = px[r] ^ px[l−1].

Worked example: Single Number III (LeetCode 260). Every number appears twice except two, a and b.

  1. XOR everything: the pairs cancel, leaving x = a ^ b (not 0, because a ≠ b).
  2. Pick a bit where a and b differ: the lowest set bit of x.
  3. Split all numbers by that bit and XOR each group. One group gives a, the other b.
vector<int> singleNumber(vector<int>& nums) {
    long long x = 0;
    for (int v : nums) x ^= v;
    long long low = x & -x;
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    for (int v : nums) (v & low) ? a ^= v : b ^= v;
    return {a, b};
}
public int[] singleNumber(int[] nums) {
    int x = 0;
    for (int v : nums) x ^= v;
    int low = x & -x;                    // safe in Java: wraps without error
    int a = 0, b = 0;
    for (int v : nums) { if ((v & low) != 0) a ^= v; else b ^= v; }
    return new int[]{a, b};
}

blocks.title: 6. Binary trie (idea for the take-home)
blocks.html: To find the maximum a ^ b in an array, insert each number's bits from the highest into a tree with two children per node (0 and 1). For each number, walk down preferring the opposite bit at each level: that greedily makes the highest bits of the XOR equal to 1. O(n × 31).

tabs.label: Stacks & monotonic stack
tabs.head: Lecture 12: Stacks & monotonic stack
tabs.lead: A monotonic stack finds, for every position, the nearest smaller (or greater) element in O(n) total.

blocks.title: 1. Stack basics
blocks.html: Last in, first out. Classic use: matching brackets. Push openers; on a closer, the top must be its partner. C++: vector or stack. Java: ArrayDeque (not the old Stack class), or a plain array with a top index.

blocks.title: 2. The monotonic stack idea
blocks.html:
To find the nearest smaller value to the left of each a[i]: keep a stack of indices whose values increase from bottom to top. Before pushing i, pop every index whose value is ≥ a[i]. They can never be anyone's answer again, because a[i] is both closer and smaller. Whatever remains on top is the answer.

Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work is O(n).

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Nearest Smaller Values
blocks.html:
CSES 1645. For each position print the nearest position to its left with a smaller value (1-based), or 0.

Dry run. a = [2, 5, 1, 4, 8, 3, 2, 5] gives 0 1 0 3 4 3 3 7.

vector<int> st;                          // indices; values increase upwards
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    while (!st.empty() && a[st.back()] >= a[i]) st.pop_back();
    cout << (st.empty() ? 0 : st.back() + 1) << ' ';
    st.push_back(i);
}
int[] st = new int[n]; int top = 0;
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
blocks.html:
LeetCode 84. Bars of width 1 and given heights. Largest rectangle?

Key idea. In the best rectangle, some bar is the shortest. For each bar, stretch left and right until a shorter bar: width = nextSmaller − prevSmaller − 1. One monotonic stack pass finds both limits when a bar is popped.

Dry run. heights = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]. Bar 5 (index 2) stretches over indices 2..3: area 5 × 2 = 10. That is the answer.

int largestRectangleArea(vector<int>& h) {
    vector<int> st; long long best = 0; int n = h.size();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : h[i];                    // height-0 sentinel flushes the stack
        while (!st.empty() && h[st.back()] > cur) {
            int height = h[st.back()]; st.pop_back();
            int left = st.empty() ? -1 : st.back();
            best = max(best, 1LL * height * (i - left - 1));
        }
        st.push_back(i);
    }
    return (int)best;
}
public int largestRectangleArea(int[] h) {
    int n = h.length; int[] st = new int[n + 1]; int top = 0; long best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : h[i];
        while (top > 0 && h[st[top - 1]] > cur) {
            int height = h[st[--top]];
            int left = top == 0 ? -1 : st[top - 1];
            best = Math.max(best, (long) height * (i - left - 1));
        }
        st[top++] = i;
    }
    return (int) best;
}

tabs.label: Deques & heaps
tabs.head: Lecture 13: Deques & heaps
tabs.lead: A monotonic deque gives the maximum of every sliding window in O(n). A heap gives the smallest (or largest) item in O(log n), again and again.

blocks.title: 1. Sliding window maximum with a deque
blocks.html:
Keep indices in the deque with values decreasing from front to back.

  1. Before adding i, pop from the back every index with value ≤ a[i] (they can never be a maximum again).
  2. Push i at the back.
  3. If the front index has left the window (≤ i − k), pop it from the front.
  4. Once i ≥ k − 1, the front holds the window maximum.

Dry run. a = [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3 gives maxima 3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7.

vector<int> maxSlidingWindow(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    deque<int> dq; vector<int> res;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); i++) {
        while (!dq.empty() && a[dq.back()] <= a[i]) dq.pop_back();
        dq.push_back(i);
        if (dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();
        if (i >= k - 1) res.push_back(a[dq.front()]);
    }
    return res;
}
public int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length; int[] res = new int[n - k + 1];
    ArrayDeque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) dq.pollLast();
        dq.addLast(i);
        if (dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) dq.pollFirst();
        if (i >= k - 1) res[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return res;
}

For the window minimum (CSES 3221), flip the comparison to ≥. Read that problem's input and output format carefully before coding.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Kth Largest Element
blocks.html:
LeetCode 215. Keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. When it grows past k, drop its smallest. At the end, its top is the k-th largest. O(n log k).

int findKthLargest(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;
    for (int x : a) { pq.push(x); if ((int)pq.size() > k) pq.pop(); }
    return pq.top();
}
public int findKthLargest(int[] a, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
    for (int x : a) { pq.add(x); if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll(); }
    return pq.peek();
}

blocks.title: 4. Two heaps for a running median
blocks.html:
• low: a max-heap with the smaller half
  • high: a min-heap with the larger half

  • Median = top of low (odd count), or the average of both tops (even count)

For a sliding window you must also delete the element that leaves. Heaps can't do that directly. Either mark it and skip it when it reaches the top (lazy deletion), or use ordered multisets instead (C++ multiset, Java TreeMap with counts).

blocks.title: 1. Pointer discipline
blocks.html:
• Draw the boxes and arrows first. Decide the order of rewiring so no node becomes unreachable.
  • Use a dummy head node: the real head may change, the dummy never does.

Reverse a list iteratively:

ListNode* reverse(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* prev = nullptr;
    while (head) { ListNode* nxt = head->next; head->next = prev; prev = head; head = nxt; }
    return prev;
}
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    while (head != null) { ListNode nxt = head.next; head.next = prev; prev = head; head = nxt; }
    return prev;
}

blocks.title: 2. Floyd's cycle detection
blocks.html: Move slow one step and fast two steps. If there is a cycle they meet inside it. Then put one pointer back at the head and move both one step at a time: they meet at the start of the cycle (LeetCode 142). O(n) time, O(1) memory.

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: LRU Cache
blocks.html:
LeetCode 146. get and put in O(1); when full, evict the least recently used key.

Design.

  • A hash map finds a key's node in O(1).
  • A doubly linked list keeps nodes in order of use: most recent at the front, least recent at the back. Moving or removing a node is O(1) when you hold a pointer to it.

Trace with capacity 2.

OperationList (front → back)Result
put(1, 1)1
put(2, 2)2, 1
get(1)1, 21
put(3, 3)3, 1evicts 2
get(2)3, 1−1
class LRUCache {
    int cap;
    list<pair<int,int>> order;                                  // front = most recent
    unordered_map<int, list<pair<int,int>>::iterator> where;
public:
    LRUCache(int capacity) : cap(capacity) {}
    int get(int key) {
        auto it = where.find(key);
        if (it == where.end()) return -1;
        order.splice(order.begin(), order, it->second);         // move to front in O(1)
        return it->second->second;
    }
    void put(int key, int value) {
        auto it = where.find(key);
        if (it != where.end()) {
            it->second->second = value;
            order.splice(order.begin(), order, it->second);
            return;
        }
        if ((int)order.size() == cap) {                         // evict least recent
            where.erase(order.back().first);
            order.pop_back();
        }
        order.push_front({key, value});
        where[key] = order.begin();
    }
};
class LRUCache {
    private static class Node { int key, val; Node prev, next; Node(int k, int v) { key = k; val = v; } }
    private final int cap;
    private final Map<Integer, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(0, 0), tail = new Node(0, 0);   // sentinels

    public LRUCache(int capacity) { cap = capacity; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; }
    private void unlink(Node x) { x.prev.next = x.next; x.next.prev = x.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node x) { x.next = head.next; x.prev = head; head.next.prev = x; head.next = x; }

    public int get(int key) {
        Node x = map.get(key);
        if (x == null) return -1;
        unlink(x); addFront(x);
        return x.val;
    }
    public void put(int key, int value) {
        Node x = map.get(key);
        if (x != null) { x.val = value; unlink(x); addFront(x); return; }
        if (map.size() == cap) { Node lru = tail.prev; unlink(lru); map.remove(lru.key); }
        x = new Node(key, value); addFront(x); map.put(key, x);
    }
}

Smallest prime factor (SPF) sieve. Store spf[x] instead of a yes/no. Then factorise any x ≤ N by dividing by spf[x] repeatedly: O(log x).

tabs.label: Modular arithmetic, fast power & nCr
tabs.head: Lecture 16: Modular arithmetic, fast power & nCr
tabs.lead: Answers that would be astronomically large are asked “modulo 10^9 + 7”. You must keep every intermediate value reduced.

blocks.title: 1. The rules
blocks.html:
OperationSafe form (MOD = 10^9 + 7)
Add(a + b) % MOD
Subtract(a − b + MOD) % MOD
Multiply(a × b) % MOD, with a and b in 64-bit
Divide by ba × inverse(b) % MOD (MOD is prime)

Two reduced values multiply to below 10^18, which fits in 64 bits. Three do not, so reduce after every product.

blocks.title: 2. Fast power
blocks.html:
Compute a^b in O(log b) by squaring: walk through the bits of b.

3^13: 13 = 1101 in binary, so 3^13 = 3^8 · 3^4 · 3^1.

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;
long long power(long long a, long long b, long long m = MOD) {
    long long r = 1; a %= m;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1) r = r * a % m;
        a = a * a % m;
        b >>= 1;
    }
    return r;
}
static final long MOD = 1_000_000_007L;
static long power(long a, long b, long m) {
    long r = 1; a %= m;
    while (b > 0) {
        if ((b & 1) == 1) r = r * a % m;
        a = a * a % m;
        b >>= 1;
    }
    return r;
}

Exponentiation II (CSES 1712) asks for a^(b^c). By Fermat's little theorem, exponents can be reduced modulo MOD − 1: answer = power(a, power(b, c, MOD − 1), MOD).

blocks.title: 3. Modular inverse
blocks.html: For a prime p and x not divisible by p: inverse(x) = x^(p−2) mod p.

blocks.title: 4. nCr for many queries
blocks.html:
Precompute factorials and inverse factorials once, then each C(n, r) is O(1).

const int MX = 1000000;
vector<long long> f(MX + 1), inv(MX + 1);
void build() {
    f[0] = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= MX; i++) f[i] = f[i-1] * i % MOD;
    inv[MX] = power(f[MX], MOD - 2);
    for (int i = MX; i > 0; i--) inv[i-1] = inv[i] * i % MOD;
}
long long C(int n, int r) { if (r < 0 || r > n) return 0; return f[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n-r] % MOD; }
static final int MX = 1_000_000;
static long[] f = new long[MX + 1], inv = new long[MX + 1];
static void build() {
    f[0] = 1; for (int i = 1; i <= MX; i++) f[i] = f[i - 1] * i % MOD;
    inv[MX] = power(f[MX], MOD - 2, MOD);
    for (int i = MX; i > 0; i--) inv[i - 1] = inv[i] * i % MOD;
}
static long C(int n, int r) { if (r < 0 || r > n) return 0; return f[n] * inv[r] % MOD * inv[n - r] % MOD; }

blocks.title: 1. Inclusion–exclusion
blocks.html:
A ∪ B=A+B−A ∩ B. With more sets, add single sets, subtract pairs, add triples, and so on.

Numbers ≤ 20 divisible by 2 or 3: 10 + 6 − 3 = 13.

Worked example: Prime Multiples (CSES 2185). Count numbers ≤ n divisible by at least one of k ≤ 20 primes. Loop over every non-empty mask of primes: multiply them (stop if the product passes n), then add n / product when the mask has an odd number of primes and subtract it when even.

long long ans = 0;
for (int m = 1; m < (1 << k); m++) {
    long long prod = 1; bool over = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if (m >> i & 1) {
        if (prod > n / p[i]) { over = true; break; }
        prod *= p[i];
    }
    if (over) continue;
    ans += (__builtin_popcount(m) % 2 ? 1 : -1) * (n / prod);
}
long ans = 0;
for (int m = 1; m < (1 << k); m++) {
    long prod = 1; boolean over = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if ((m >> i & 1) == 1) {
        if (prod > n / p[i]) { over = true; break; }
        prod *= p[i];
    }
    if (over) continue;
    ans += (Integer.bitCount(m) % 2 == 1 ? 1 : -1) * (n / prod);
}

blocks.title: 2. Matrix exponentiation
blocks.html:
A recurrence like F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2) is a matrix multiplication:

[F(n+1) ; F(n)] = [1 1 ; 1 0] [F(n) ; F(n-1)]

So F(n) comes from the n-th power of that matrix, computed by fast power in O(log n) matrix products. This handles n up to 10^18 (CSES 1722). A recurrence using the last k terms needs a k × k matrix: O(k³ log n).

blocks.title: 3. Worked example: Lowest Common Ancestor
blocks.html:
LeetCode 236. f(node) returns p or q if it finds one in this subtree, or the LCA once both are found, otherwise null.

TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
    if (!root || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode* L = lowestCommonAncestor(root->left, p, q);
    TreeNode* R = lowestCommonAncestor(root->right, p, q);
    if (L && R) return root;           // p and q are on different sides
    return L ? L : R;
}
public TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode L = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode R = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (L != null && R != null) return root;
    return L != null ? L : R;
}

blocks.title: 4. Worked example: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
blocks.html:
LeetCode 124. A path may bend once, at its highest node.

  • gain(node) returns the best downward path starting at node: node.val + max(0, gain(left), gain(right)).
  • At each node, a bent path left → node → right could be the answer: update the global best.
int best = INT_MIN;
int gain(TreeNode* x) {
    if (!x) return 0;
    int l = max(0, gain(x->left)), r = max(0, gain(x->right));
    best = max(best, x->val + l + r);          // path bending at x
    return x->val + max(l, r);                 // only one branch goes up
}
int maxPathSum(TreeNode* root) { gain(root); return best; }
int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
int gain(TreeNode x) {
    if (x == null) return 0;
    int l = Math.max(0, gain(x.left)), r = Math.max(0, gain(x.right));
    best = Math.max(best, x.val + l + r);
    return x.val + Math.max(l, r);
}
public int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) { gain(root); return best; }

Deep trees. A chain of 2 × 10^5 nodes can overflow the recursion stack. Safer: BFS from the root to get an order where parents come first, then process that order backwards for anything computed from children.

blocks.title: 3. Diameter: the longest path
blocks.html:
1. BFS from any node; let u be the farthest node.
  2. BFS from u; the farthest distance is the diameter.

Why it works: the farthest node from anywhere is always an end of some longest path.

blocks.title: 4. Euler tour
blocks.html: Number nodes when DFS enters (tin) and leaves (tout). The subtree of v is exactly the nodes with tin in [tin[v], tout[v]]. This turns subtree questions into range questions (used with Fenwick trees in Lecture 34).

blocks.title: 1. The idea
blocks.html:
Store, for every node, its ancestor 1, 2, 4, 8, … levels up:

up[j][v] = up[j-1][ up[j-1][v] ]

The 2^j-th ancestor is the 2^(j−1)-th ancestor of the 2^(j−1)-th ancestor. With 18 levels you can jump up to 2^18 > 2 × 10^5 steps. Building the table is O(n log n); each query is O(log n).

blocks.title: 2. K-th ancestor
blocks.html: Write k in binary and jump once for each set bit. k = 13 = 8 + 4 + 1: jump 8, then 4, then 1.

blocks.title: 3. Lowest common ancestor
blocks.html:
1. Lift the deeper node until both have the same depth.
  2. If they are now the same node, that's the LCA.
  3. Otherwise, from the biggest jump down to the smallest, jump both nodes whenever their ancestors differ.
  4. Their parent is the LCA.
const int LOG = 18;
vector<array<int, LOG>> up;   // up[v][j]
vector<int> dep;
int kth(int v, int k) { for (int j = 0; j < LOG && v; j++) if (k >> j & 1) v = up[v][j]; return v; }
int lca(int a, int b) {
    if (dep[a] < dep[b]) swap(a, b);
    a = kth(a, dep[a] - dep[b]);
    if (a == b) return a;
    for (int j = LOG - 1; j >= 0; j--) if (up[a][j] != up[b][j]) { a = up[a][j]; b = up[b][j]; }
    return up[a][0];
}
static final int LOG = 18; static int[][] up; static int[] dep;     // up[j][v]
static int kth(int v, int k) { for (int j = 0; j < LOG && v != 0; j++) if ((k >> j & 1) == 1) v = up[j][v]; return v; }
static int lca(int a, int b) {
    if (dep[a] < dep[b]) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
    a = kth(a, dep[a] - dep[b]);
    if (a == b) return a;
    for (int j = LOG - 1; j >= 0; j--) if (up[j][a] != up[j][b]) { a = up[j][a]; b = up[j][b]; }
    return up[0][a];
}

Use 0 as “no ancestor” (the root's parent is 0 and 0's parent is 0). In Company Queries I, print −1 when the jump lands on 0.

blocks.title: 4. What LCA unlocks
blocks.html:
• Distance: dist(u, v) = depth[u] + depth[v] − 2 · depth[lca(u, v)]
  • Add 1 to every node on the path u–v: +1 at u and v, −1 at the LCA and at the LCA's parent, then sum each subtree (Counting Paths)

intro: First question for every graph problem: what are the nodes, what are the edges, are edges directed, and do they have weights? Once you can answer that, the algorithm usually follows.

blocks.title: 1. Storing a graph
blocks.html:
Use an adjacency list: for each node, the list of its neighbours. Memory O(n + m). An adjacency matrix (n × n) only works for n up to a few thousand.

vector<vector<int>> g(n + 1);
for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { int a, b; cin >> a >> b; g[a].push_back(b); g[b].push_back(a); }
List<Integer>[] g = new ArrayList[n + 1];
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) g[i] = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < m; i++) { int a = nextInt(), b = nextInt(); g[a].add(b); g[b].add(a); }

blocks.title: 2. BFS: shortest paths when every edge costs the same
blocks.html:
BFS visits nodes in order of distance. Mark a node visited when you push it. Keep parent to rebuild the path.

vector<int> dist(n + 1, -1), par(n + 1, 0); queue<int> q; dist[s] = 0; q.push(s);
while (!q.empty()) { int u = q.front(); q.pop();
    for (int v : g[u]) if (dist[v] == -1) { dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; par[v] = u; q.push(v); } }
int[] dist = new int[n + 1], par = new int[n + 1]; Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
ArrayDeque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>(); dist[s] = 0; q.add(s);
while (!q.isEmpty()) { int u = q.poll();
    for (int v : g[u]) if (dist[v] == -1) { dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; par[v] = u; q.add(v); } }

To print the path to t: follow par from t back to s, then reverse.

blocks.title: 3. Grids are graphs
blocks.html:
Each cell is a node; neighbours are up, down, left, right. Use direction arrays and a bounds check.

  • Counting Rooms (CSES 1192): count how many times you start a new BFS/flood fill from an unvisited floor cell.
  • Labyrinth (CSES 1193): BFS from A; remember the direction letter used to enter each cell; walk back from B and reverse the letters.

Avoid recursive flood fill on a 1000 × 1000 grid: a million nested calls overflow the stack.

  • A graph is bipartite if you can colour nodes with two colours so every edge joins different colours. BFS colouring finds a conflict if it isn't (Building Teams).

blocks.title: 1. Topological order (Kahn's algorithm)
blocks.html:
Order tasks so every task comes after its prerequisites.

  1. Count incoming edges (in-degree) for every node.
  2. Put all nodes with in-degree 0 in a queue.
  3. Pop a node, add it to the order, and decrease its neighbours' in-degrees; push any that reach 0.
  4. If fewer than n nodes come out, there is a cycle: no valid order.

Course Schedule (CSES 1679) is exactly this; print IMPOSSIBLE on a cycle.

vector<int> indeg(n + 1, 0), order;
for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++) for (int v : g[u]) indeg[v]++;
queue<int> q; for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++) if (indeg[u] == 0) q.push(u);
while (!q.empty()) { int u = q.front(); q.pop(); order.push_back(u);
    for (int v : g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v); }
int[] indeg = new int[n + 1];
for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++) for (int v : g[u]) indeg[v]++;
ArrayDeque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>(); for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++) if (indeg[u] == 0) q.add(u);
List<Integer> order = new ArrayList<>();
while (!q.isEmpty()) { int u = q.poll(); order.add(u);
    for (int v : g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.add(v); }

blocks.title: 2. Finding cycles
blocks.html:
• Undirected: during DFS, reaching a visited node that isn't your parent means a cycle.
  • Directed: colour nodes white (new), grey (on the current DFS path), black (finished). An edge to a grey node is a cycle. Keep parents to print it.

blocks.title: 3. DP on a DAG
blocks.html:
Process nodes in topological order; every predecessor is finished before you use it.

  • Longest path: best[v] = max over edges u → v of best[u] + 1
  • Number of paths from 1: ways[v] = sum over edges u → v of ways[u]
  • Mark nodes unreachable from the start as −∞, not 0 (Longest Flight Route)

SituationUseTime

blocks.title: 2. Dijkstra
blocks.html:
Always expand the closest unfinished node. With a priority queue, push (distance, node) whenever you improve a distance, and skip entries that are out of date when popped.

Shortest Routes I (CSES 1671): distances from city 1 to all cities. Use 64-bit distances.

vector<long long> dist(n + 1, LLONG_MAX); dist[1] = 0;
priority_queue<pair<long long,int>, vector<pair<long long,int>>, greater<>> pq; pq.push({0, 1});
while (!pq.empty()) {
    auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
    if (d > dist[u]) continue;                         // out-of-date entry
    for (auto [v, w] : g[u])
        if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.push({dist[v], v}); }
}
long[] dist = new long[n + 1]; Arrays.fill(dist, Long.MAX_VALUE); dist[1] = 0;
PriorityQueue<long[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) -> Long.compare(x[0], y[0]));
pq.add(new long[]{0, 1});
while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
    long[] t = pq.poll(); long d = t[0]; int u = (int) t[1];
    if (d > dist[u]) continue;
    for (int[] e : g[u]) { int v = e[0]; long w = e[1];
        if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.add(new long[]{dist[v], v}); } }
}

Negative edges break Dijkstra: a node already finished might later be reachable more cheaply.

blocks.title: 3. Floyd–Warshall
blocks.html: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) with k in the outer loop. Answers all pairs (Shortest Routes II).

blocks.title: 4. Bellman–Ford
blocks.html: Relax every edge n − 1 times. If anything still improves in an n-th round, a negative cycle exists. In High Score a bad cycle only matters if it can reach the destination.

blocks.title: 5. Extra state = bigger graph

blocks.title: 1. Disjoint Set Union
blocks.html:
Keeps track of which items are in the same group, with almost O(1) find and unite.

struct DSU {
    vector<int> p, sz;
    DSU(int n) : p(n + 1), sz(n + 1, 1) { iota(p.begin(), p.end(), 0); }
    int find(int x) { while (p[x] != x) { p[x] = p[p[x]]; x = p[x]; } return x; }
    bool unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b); if (a == b) return false;
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) swap(a, b);
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; return true;
    }
};
static int[] p, sz;
static int find(int x) { while (p[x] != x) { p[x] = p[p[x]]; x = p[x]; } return x; }
static boolean unite(int a, int b) {
    a = find(a); b = find(b); if (a == b) return false;
    if (sz[a] < sz[b]) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
    p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; return true;
}

Road Construction (CSES 1676): after each road, print the number of components and the largest component size. Every successful unite reduces the count by 1.

blocks.title: 2. Minimum spanning tree (Kruskal)
blocks.html:
Connect all n nodes with n − 1 edges of minimum total cost:

  1. Sort edges by cost.
  2. Take each edge whose ends are in different groups (unite them).
  3. If you took fewer than n − 1 edges, the graph is disconnected (Road Reparation: IMPOSSIBLE).

For dense graphs (every pair of points), Prim's O(n²) version without a heap is simpler and faster.

blocks.title: 1. Strongly connected components
blocks.html:
In a directed graph, an SCC is a largest group where every node can reach every other. Kosaraju's algorithm:

  1. DFS the graph; record nodes in the order they finish.
  2. Reverse every edge.
  3. Go through nodes in reverse finish order; each DFS on the reversed graph from an unassigned node collects exactly one SCC.

Shrinking each SCC to one node gives a DAG (the condensation), so you can run DAG DP on it (Coin Collector).

Quick check, one SCC or not (Flight Routes Check): BFS from node 1 in the graph and in the reversed graph. If both reach everything, the whole graph is one SCC; otherwise print a pair that fails.

blocks.title: 2. Bridges and articulation points
blocks.html:
In an undirected graph, a bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph; an articulation point is such a vertex.

During DFS record tin[v] (entry time) and low[v] = the smallest tin reachable from v's subtree using at most one back edge.

  • Edge (p, c) is a bridge if low[c] > tin[p].
  • Vertex p (not the root) is an articulation point if some child has low[c] ≥ tin[p]. The root is one if it has two or more DFS children.

Skip only the exact edge you arrived by (use edge ids), so parallel edges are handled correctly.

intro:
Dynamic programming = solve each small subproblem once, store it, and build bigger answers from smaller ones. Use the DP card below for every problem in this module.

blocks.title: 1. From recursion to a table

blocks.title: 2. Worked example: Frog 1

AtCoder DP A. A frog jumps from stone i to i+1 or i+2, paying |h_i − h_j|. Minimum total cost to reach stone n?

PartFrog 1

blocks.title: 3. Counting vs optimising
blocks.html:
• Counting (how many ways): add the smaller states, modulo 10^9 + 7. Dice Combinations: dp[s] = dp[s−1] + … + dp[s−6], dp[0] = 1.
  • Optimising (min/max): take the best of the smaller states. Minimizing Coins: dp[s] = 1 + min over coins c of dp[s − c], with dp[0] = 0 and “impossible” marked as a large value.

blocks.title: 1. 0/1 knapsack
blocks.html:
Each item has weight w and value v and can be taken once. dp[c] = best value with capacity c. For each item, loop c downwards so the item isn't used twice.

Book Shop: price = weight, pages = value.

vector<int> dp(x + 1, 0);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int c = x; c >= price[i]; c--)
        dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - price[i]] + pages[i]);
cout << dp[x] << '\n';

    for (int c = x; c >= price[i]; c--)

blocks.html:
dp[i][j] = LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j of b.

  • If a[i] = b[j]: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1
  • Otherwise: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1])

blocks.title: 2. Edit distance

CSES 1639. Fewest insertions, deletions and replacements to turn a into b.

dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j] + 1, dp[i][j-1] + 1, dp[i-1][j-1] + [ai ≠ bj])

Base: dp[i][0] = i, dp[0][j] = j.

for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) dp[i][0] = i;
for (int j = 0; j <= m; j++) dp[0][j] = j;

blocks.title: 3. Longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n)
blocks.html:
Keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each x, find the first tail ≥ x (lower bound) and replace it with x, or append x if none. The length of tails is the answer. (tails is not itself a valid subsequence.)

vector<int> t;
for (int x : a) {
    auto it = lower_bound(t.begin(), t.end(), x);
    if (it == t.end()) t.push_back(x); else *it = x;
}
int[] t = new int[n]; int len = 0;
for (int x : a) {
    int lo = -1, hi = len;
    while (hi - lo > 1) { int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1; if (t[mid] >= x) hi = mid; else lo = mid; }
    t[hi] = x; if (hi == len) len++;
}

blocks.title: 1. Interval DP
blocks.html:
State over a range: dp[l][r] = best answer for a[l..r]. Fill by increasing length, so shorter ranges are ready.

Deque (AtCoder DP L): two players take from either end. dp[l][r] = (my score − opponent's) when it's my turn on a[l..r]:

dp[l][r] = max(al - dp[l+1][r], ar - dp[l][r-1])

Slimes (AtCoder DP N): merging l..r ends with one final merge at some split k: dp[l][r] = min over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k+1][r] + sum(l..r). O(n³).

Last-operation trick (Burst Balloons): instead of choosing what happens first, choose which element is handled last in the interval. Then the two sides are independent.

blocks.title: 2. DP on trees
blocks.html:
Compute each node from its children (post-order). Independent Set (AtCoder DP P): count colourings where no two black nodes are adjacent.

  • white[v] = Π over children (white[c] + black[c])
  • black[v] = Π over children white[c]

House Robber III is the same shape with max and + instead of + and ×.

blocks.title: 1. Bitmask DP
blocks.html:
When n ≤ 20, the set of items already used fits in a mask, and 2^20 ≈ 10^6 masks is affordable.

Matching (AtCoder DP O): match n men with n women (compatible pairs given). dp[mask] = ways to match the first popcount(mask) men to exactly the women in mask.

vector<long long> dp(1 << n, 0); dp[0] = 1;
for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
    int man = __builtin_popcount(mask);          // next man to match
    if (man >= n || !dp[mask]) continue;
    for (int w = 0; w < n; w++)
        if (ok[man][w] && !(mask >> w & 1)) dp[mask | 1 << w] = (dp[mask | 1 << w] + dp[mask]) % MOD;
}
cout << dp[(1 << n) - 1] << '\n';
long[] dp = new long[1 << n]; dp[0] = 1;
for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {
    int man = Integer.bitCount(mask);
    if (man >= n || dp[mask] == 0) continue;
    for (int w = 0; w < n; w++)
        if (ok[man][w] && (mask >> w & 1) == 0) dp[mask | 1 << w] = (dp[mask | 1 << w] + dp[mask]) % MOD;
}
out.println(dp[(1 << n) - 1]);

Paths through every node (Hamiltonian Flights): dp[mask][v] = ways to start at 1, visit exactly mask, and stand at v. About 2 × 10^7 states: use int arrays and skip masks without city 1.

blocks.title: 2. Digit DP
blocks.html:
Count numbers ≤ K with some digit property, when K is huge (even 10^10000 as a string). Build the number digit by digit:

  • pos: which digit you're choosing
  • tight: is the prefix so far equal to K's prefix? If so, the next digit can't exceed K's digit
  • state: whatever the property needs (digit sum mod D, previous digit, count of non-zero digits…)

To count in [L, R], compute f(R) − f(L − 1).

blocks.title: 2. Sparse table
blocks.html: st[k][i] = min of a[i .. i + 2^k − 1], built as min(st[k−1][i], st[k−1][i + 2^(k−1)]). For a query [l, r], take k = ⌊log2(r − l + 1)⌋ and combine two blocks that overlap: min(st[k][l], st[k][r − 2^k + 1]). Overlap is fine for min/max, not for sums. (CSES 1647)

blocks.title: 3. Fenwick tree
blocks.html:
Position i (1-based) stores the sum of the last (i & −i) elements ending at i. Prefix sums walk down by removing the lowest bit; updates walk up by adding it.

struct BIT {
    int n; vector<long long> t;
    BIT(int n) : n(n), t(n + 1, 0) {}
    void add(int i, long long v) { for (; i <= n; i += i & -i) t[i] += v; }
    long long sum(int i) { long long s = 0; for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += t[i]; return s; }
    long long sum(int l, int r) { return sum(r) - sum(l - 1); }
};
static long[] t; static int N;
static void add(int i, long v) { for (; i <= N; i += i & -i) t[i] += v; }
static long sum(int i) { long s = 0; for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) s += t[i]; return s; }
static long sum(int l, int r) { return sum(r) - sum(l - 1); }

Dynamic Range Sum Queries (CSES 1648): “set position k to u” becomes add(k, u − a[k]); then a[k] = u.

blocks.title: 4. Fenwick tricks
blocks.html:
• Range add, point query: keep a BIT on the difference array: add(l, v), add(r + 1, −v); the value at i is sum(i). (Range Update Queries)
  • Counting smaller elements: compress values to ranks 1..n, scan from the right, query sum(rank − 1), then add(rank, 1).
  • Subtree sums: with an Euler tour (Lecture 19) each subtree is a contiguous range.

blocks.title: 1. The structure
blocks.html:
A binary tree over the array: each node stores the answer for its range, combined from its two children. Query by covering [l, r] with O(log n) nodes; update a leaf and fix its ancestors.

int n; vector<long long> tr;            // size 4n, recursive
void update(int node, int l, int r, int pos, long long val) {
    if (l == r) { tr[node] = val; return; }
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    if (pos <= m) update(2*node, l, m, pos, val); else update(2*node+1, m+1, r, pos, val);
    tr[node] = min(tr[2*node], tr[2*node+1]);
}
long long query(int node, int l, int r, int ql, int qr) {
    if (qr < l || r < ql) return LLONG_MAX;
    if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tr[node];
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    return min(query(2*node, l, m, ql, qr), query(2*node+1, m+1, r, ql, qr));
}
static long[] tr;                       // size 4n
static void update(int node, int l, int r, int pos, long val) {
    if (l == r) { tr[node] = val; return; }
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    if (pos <= m) update(2*node, l, m, pos, val); else update(2*node+1, m+1, r, pos, val);
    tr[node] = Math.min(tr[2*node], tr[2*node+1]);
}
static long query(int node, int l, int r, int ql, int qr) {
    if (qr < l || r < ql) return Long.MAX_VALUE;
    if (ql <= l && r <= qr) return tr[node];
    int m = (l + r) / 2;
    return Math.min(query(2*node, l, m, ql, qr), query(2*node+1, m+1, r, ql, qr));
}

blocks.title: 2. Walking down the tree
blocks.html: Hotel Queries: find the first hotel with at least x free rooms. Store the maximum per node; from the root, go left if the left child's maximum ≥ x, otherwise right. O(log n), no binary search needed.

blocks.title: 3. Designing your own node
blocks.html:
Ask: what must each node store so two neighbours can be merged? For the best subarray sum (Subarray Sum Queries), store sum, best prefix, best suffix and best:

  • best = max(L.best, R.best, L.suffix + R.prefix)
  • prefix = max(L.prefix, L.sum + R.prefix), suffix = max(R.suffix, R.sum + L.suffix)

blocks.title: 4. Lazy propagation
blocks.html: To add v to a whole range, don't touch every leaf. Mark the covering nodes with a pending “+v” (the lazy tag) and update their stored value. Before visiting a node's children, push its tag down. If you support both “add” and “set”, a set overrides any pending add.

tabs.lead: Checking a pattern at every position of a text is O(n · m). These tools do it in O(n + m).

blocks.title: 1. Pick the tool
blocks.html:
TaskTool

Borders, periods of a stringPrefix function / Z-function

blocks.title: 2. Prefix function
blocks.html:
π[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of s[0..i] that is also a suffix of it.

i0123456
saabaaab
π0101223
vector<int> prefixFunction(const string& s) {
    int n = s.size(); vector<int> pi(n, 0);
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int k = pi[i-1];
        while (k > 0 && s[i] != s[k]) k = pi[k-1];
        if (s[i] == s[k]) k++;
        pi[i] = k;
    }
    return pi;
}
static int[] prefixFunction(String s) {
    int n = s.length(); int[] pi = new int[n];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        int k = pi[i - 1];
        while (k > 0 && s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(k)) k = pi[k - 1];
        if (s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(k)) k++;
        pi[i] = k;
    }
    return pi;
}

Counting occurrences (String Matching): compute π of pattern + '#' + text; every position where π equals the pattern length is a match.

All borders (Finding Borders): start with k = π[n−1] and follow k = π[k−1] until 0.

blocks.title: 3. Z-function
blocks.html: z[i] = length of the longest common prefix of s and the suffix starting at i. p is a period of s exactly when z[p] = n − p (and p = n always works). (Finding Periods)

blocks.title: 4. Rolling hash
blocks.html: Treat a string as a number in base B modulo a big prime M. With prefix hashes h and powers pw, the hash of s[l..r) is (h[r] − h[l] · pw[r − l]) mod M. Two equal substrings always have equal hashes; unequal ones collide rarely. Use a random base, and two different moduli when it matters.

blocks.title: 5. Trie
blocks.html:
A tree where each edge is a letter and each root-to-node path is a prefix. Insert and search cost O(word length). Store children as an array of 26.

struct Trie {
    vector<array<int, 26>> nxt{{}}; vector<bool> end{false};
    void insert(const string& w) { int v = 0;
        for (char ch : w) { int c = ch - 'a';
            if (!nxt[v][c]) { nxt[v][c] = nxt.size(); nxt.push_back({}); end.push_back(false); }
            v = nxt[v][c]; }
        end[v] = true; }
};
static int[][] nxt = new int[1_000_001][26]; static boolean[] end = new boolean[1_000_001]; static int cnt = 1;
static void insert(String w) { int v = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < w.length(); i++) { int c = w.charAt(i) - 'a';
        if (nxt[v][c] == 0) nxt[v][c] = cnt++;
        v = nxt[v][c]; }
    end[v] = true; }

Size the Java arrays to the total length of all words plus one.

Word Combinations (CSES 1731): dp[i] = ways to build the suffix starting at i. From each i, walk the trie along s[i..]; whenever you hit a word end at j, add dp[j + 1].

blocks.title: 6. Palindromes
blocks.html: Expand around each centre (n odd centres, n − 1 even ones): O(n²), fine for n ≤ 1000 (LeetCode 5). For n = 10^6 use Manacher's algorithm (CSES 1111).

name: M11 Placement readiness
title: M11 Placement Readiness: Student Handbook
intro: The last four lectures turn your DSA skill into offers: online assessments, design rounds, interviews and your resume.

blocks.title: 1. What to expect
blocks.html: Usually 2–3 problems in 60–90 minutes on a HackerRank- or HackerEarth-style platform. Hidden tests, partial credit for tests passed, often no autocomplete, sometimes webcam proctoring.

blocks.title: 2. OA playbook
blocks.html:
1. Read everything first (5 minutes). Rank problems by how sure you are.
  2. Bank points early: solve the one you're surest of first.
  3. No idea in 10 minutes? Submit a correct brute force for partial credit, then improve it.
  4. Test before submitting: n = 1, duplicates, negatives, largest sizes, empty input.
  5. Watch the clock: an untouched problem is worth more than polishing a solved one.

blocks.title: 3. Which module does this question come from?
blocks.html:
If you see…ThinkModule
“number of subarrays with sum/property…”Prefix sums + hashingM1
“longest substring/subarray such that…”Sliding windowM1
“minimum capacity / speed / days to…”Binary search on the answerM2
“schedule / rooms / k largest…”Heap greedyM4
“islands, maze, groups, connections…”BFS / DSUM7
“number of ways / minimum cost to reach…”DPM8

blocks.title: 1. What interviewers check
blocks.html: Can you turn a vague request (“design a parking lot”) into clean classes with clear responsibilities, and explain trade-offs?

blocks.title: 2. The five-step answer
blocks.html:
1. Clarify requirements and what's out of scope.
  2. List entities and what each is responsible for.
  3. Draw relationships: has-a (composition) before is-a (inheritance).
  4. Define the main methods and the data structures behind them.
  5. Discuss extension, concurrency (two users, one resource) and failure cases.

blocks.title: 3. SOLID in one line each
blocks.html:
PrincipleMeaning
Single responsibilityA class has one reason to change
Open/closedAdd behaviour by adding code, not editing old code
Liskov substitutionA subclass must work wherever its parent does
Interface segregationSmall, focused interfaces
Dependency inversionDepend on interfaces, not concrete classes

blocks.title: 4. Patterns you should recognise
blocks.html:
• Strategy: swap an algorithm at runtime (LRU vs LFU eviction in Project 1)
  • Observer: notify subscribers when something changes
  • Factory: create the right object type from input (Car, Bike, Truck)
  • Singleton: exactly one shared instance (configuration); use sparingly

blocks.title: 1. Think aloud: the 7 steps
blocks.html:
1. Restate the problem; ask about constraints and edge cases.
  2. Work a small example by hand.
  3. Give a brute force and its complexity.
  4. Improve it and name the pattern.
  5. Code cleanly while explaining.
  6. Dry-run your code; test edge cases.
  7. State the final time and space complexity.

blocks.title: 3. Behavioural answers (STAR)
blocks.html: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Prepare five stories: a conflict, a failure, leading something, a tight deadline, and a project deep-dive (your capstone works well).
